overview: The Sultanate of Aïr, centred on Agadez in present-day Niger, connected Saharan caravan routes with a distinctive urban society. Its history survives in earthen houses, mosques, craft traditions and continuing local institutions.

periods.title: A caravan capital and earthen city
periods.summary: Agadez developed as the sultanate’s capital during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Its neighbourhood pattern retained the outlines of earlier encampments as communities settled in the city.

periods.title: Colonial rule and a changed sultanate
periods.summary: French troops took Agadez in 1904. The sultan supported the Kaossen revolt of 1916 to 1917. The institution subsequently continued in an intermediary role under colonial rule.

periods.title: Continuity within independent Niger
periods.summary: After Niger became independent in 1960, the sultanate retained a local social and political role. This continuity did not restore a separate sovereign state.

items.text: Agadez’s irregular neighbourhoods preserve the outlines of earlier Tuareg encampments. Streets, houses and shared spaces therefore record how settlement grew through existing social groupings. The surviving plan is evidence of an urban history shaped by communities as well as by rulers.

Traditional houses are built around courtyards that admit light and air. The entrance vestibule can receive visitors, accommodate grain pounding, or support craft production and sales. Earthen benches beside doorways provide seating and help protect wall bases. Domestic architecture joined household work, sociability and maintenance.

Measured study of the Great Mosque identified successive building campaigns rather than a single original design. Cressier proposed an early prayer hall before 1449 and an eastern enlargement before 1515. His reconstruction combines dimensions, surviving fabric, written references and oral tradition; the dates remain approximate.

The mosque’s later minaret should not be presented as untouched medieval fabric. Cressier proposed a major nineteenth-century campaign around 1844 or 1847. Rebuilding and continued use are part of the monument’s history, and explain why the visible structure contains evidence from different periods.

The historic centre’s importance extends beyond the palace and mosque to its many earthen dwellings. UNESCO’s assessment identifies neighbourhood chiefs and committees as part of local protection. Keeping a living city usable involves residents and everyday repairs alongside the conservation of celebrated monuments.

Agadez depended on exchange with farming regions as well as on long-distance caravans. Baier’s study of neighbouring Damergu describes villagers taking millet to Agadez, then increasingly sending it south toward Nigeria after 1900. The change connects the desert city’s fortunes to cultivators and the movement of staple food.

The same study describes villagers exchanging tanned goat skins and ostrich feathers for imported cloth and other goods. When trans-Saharan commerce declined, grain and livestock became more important. These are documented regional responses to changing demand, not evidence that every household in the sultanate followed one occupation.

An Agadez-cross ornament at the Musée des Confluences, inventory 2015.32.3, is catalogued as a twentieth-century silver-alloy piece from Azawagh, associated with Iwellemmeden Kel-Denneg Tuareg. Its name connects it with a recognizable regional jewellery form, but does not prove manufacture in Agadez or under its medieval sultans.

The museum records the ornament’s collection between 1990 and 2011 and its later donation. It describes the form as worn mainly by women in necklaces and ear ornaments. These details document use and collecting history while leaving this particular object’s maker and exact manufacture date unidentified.

A recent conservation project used photographs to build three-dimensional records of the Great Mosque and historic homes, including the Baker’s House. Local representatives learned documentation techniques. The resulting records help plan repairs and preserve measurable evidence of buildings whose earthen surfaces change through weathering and maintenance.

Local craftspeople made fitted leather bags for manuscripts kept at the Abawagé mosque, replacing damaged protective coverings. This project links leatherworking with the care of written knowledge. The conservation account documents the intervention, but does not provide dates or contents for every manuscript.

House rehabilitation included crack repair, wall-base reinforcement, replastering, roof work and improved drainage. Young residents learned from masons while occupied homes were repaired. The project’s 2021 campaign shows the continuation of building knowledge through paid work and training, as well as through the monuments themselves.

ending.text: French occupation changed the sultanate’s political position. The revolt of 1916 to 1917 challenged colonial control, but the institution continued afterward and within independent Niger. Loss of sovereignty was not the disappearance of Agadez’s communities or the abolition of every local office.
